title: Taylor’s $31bn in budget savings
full_text:
Angus Taylor has revealed the Coalition will more than offset the cost of its signature income tax cuts with $31bn in budget savings, ramping up pressure on Labor to cut spending ahead of an expected interest rate rise next month.
The Opposition Leader on Monday will release costings showing his policy to increase income tax thresholds in line with inflation has been fully funded, with the budget a net $22bn better off over four years from the 2028 election year.
The net figure to be released by the Coalition includes its planned savings and the income tax package, but does not include other measures that will impact the budget, including its vow to repeal Labor’s tax cuts and lower the fuel excise every time oil trades at over $100 a barrel.
The Australian understands Mr Taylor is planning on unveiling further savings in the coming months to establish fiscal credibility, while planning to go to the election with a better bottom line than Anthony Albanese and Jim Chalmers.
The Coalition costings come as a delegation of small business leaders will descend on Canberra this week to pressure the government over its trusts tax package before parliament, while Labor will turn the heat on to Mr Taylor over his opposition to the free-trade agreement with the European Union.
With the Treasurer under pressure to unveil sharp cuts to government spending in the mid-year budget update to assist the Reserve Bank in tackling elevated inflation, Mr Taylor said “Labor’s answer is higher taxes and more spending”.
“Labor can’t manage money and One Nation can’t explain how it would pay for its promises,” he said. “The Coalition has done the hard work, found the savings and shown how we’ll fund lower taxes.” The Coalition is claiming what it had identified would take enough pressure off inflation to avoid an interest rate increase, with markets expecting the RBA to raise the cash rate in its November or December meetings.
While the Treasurer has flagged his own savings package in next month’s mid-year budget update, it is unlikely to represent cuts of a level that would represent a major change in the government’s economic agenda.
Dr Chalmers used a speech last week to flag MYEFO would include downgrades to budget revenues and employment levels due to rising interest rates, the impact of the Iran war and high bond yields.
He also warned that global oil prices were unlikely to return to pre-Iran war levels until 2030.
“Markets now expect multiple interest rate rises in every major advanced economy over the next 12 months,” Dr Chalmers told a CITI conference last week.
Costings released by the Coalition show axing net-zero initiatives would save $9.4bn over four years, which includes an end to tax breaks and subsidies to home batteries and electric vehicles.
There would also be $7.3bn saved from “ending Labor’s corporate welfare”, including the National Reconstruction Fund and production tax credits for green hydrogen, green aluminium and critical minerals.
The Coalition would raise $4.7bn to axe Labor’s housing programs, $2bn from ending welfare for non-citizens and $7.9bn by cutting the tobacco excise.
The net impact of the Coalition’s income tax package would be a $9.7bn hit to the budget over four years, given Mr Taylor’s plan to repeal Labor’s $250-a-year end-of financial year tax rebate for workers.
However, while the Coalition has found savings to offset its tax cuts over four years, the policy is not in full flight until the final year of that period, and it is estimated to cost more than $200bn over a decade.
Under the income tax policy unveiled in Mr Taylor’s budget reply speech in May, a Coalition government would peg the bottom two tax thresholds to inflation from 2028-29 with workers to receive an initial yearly benefit of $250.
The top two thresholds for workers earning more than $135,000 would be indexed from 2031-32.
Labor is claiming Mr Taylor’s policies would increase budget deficits by nearly $140bn over four years, which includes the Coalition’s opposition to budget tax hikes, the private health insurance rebate reforms and superannuation changes.
Business owner Joseph Daoud, chief executive of advocacy group Stop the Ambition Tax, will lead a delegation to Canberra this week to meet with Liberal, Nationals, One Nation and independent MPs. The group says its polling of 514 business owners and decision-makers shows 84 per cent believe the government is not doing enough for private enterprise, while 74 per cent disapprove of Dr Chalmers’ performance as Treasurer.
With the Coalition facing calls from major business groups to backflip on its opposition to the EU free-trade agreement, the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry is leading a delegation to Singapore to encourage more trade between the nations.
The trip, funded by the Albanese government’s Accessing New Markets Initiative unveiled in response to US President Donald Trump’s tariffs, will include meetings with Singapore government representatives and business figures.
Writing in The Australian, ACCI chief executive Andrew McKellar said the trip was coming “as others question the merits of free and open trade”.
“Today one in four Australian jobs is trade-related, and nearly a third of our economic output is supported by trade,” he writes. “At a time when the rules of global commerce feel as though they are being rewritten in real time, Singapore is not just a stable partner with open markets and deep pools of capital; it is a trusted friend. For exporters across Australia this is not abstract. It is about whether there is another customer, another supplier, another source of finance when conditions change, as they so often have in recent years.”
